meta.title: AI-Enhanced Spatial Reconstruction in Thin Plastic Scintillators for Compact Space Weather Monitors

abstract: Space Weather (SW) describes the dynamic conditions of the near-Earth space environment driven by solar activity, including solar energetic particles (SEPs), which can affect spacecraft electronics and astronaut safety. Compact radiation monitors capable of discriminating between gamma rays and charged particles are essential for future SW missions. Plastic scintillator tiles are standard in anticoincidence systems for gamma-ray instruments, the chargedparticle flux they detect can offer critical tracking information if the impact position is accurately reconstructed. This work investigates the performance of different Machine Learning (ML) architectures in reconstructing the impact parameters of Minimum Ionizing Particles (MIPs). Leveraging a high-fidelity Geant4 simulation that accounts for SiPM-specific stochastic noise (crosstalk, afterpulsing, and dark counts), we compare a Center-of-Gravity baseline, a fully-connected regressor, a geometry-constrained variant of it, and a gradient-boosted tree ensemble on the mapping from eight SiPM amplitudes to the impact coordinates. The median radial error drops from 2.03 cm for the analytical baseline to 0.57 cm for gradient boosting, a factor 3.6 improvement.

blocks.html: The increasing reliance on orbital infrastructure for telecommunications, navigation, and Earth observation has heightened the demand for robust Space Weather (SW) monitoring. High-energy radiation environments pose significant risks to both spacecraft electronics and human crews; consequently, developing compact, high-efficiency radiation monitors is a priority for the New Space industry.

In this context, we present a multi-modal CubeSat instrument designed for the simultaneous detection of lowenergy gamma-rays (from 50 keV to 10 MeV) and charged particles. The core of the detector consists of a 3 × 3 × 3 matrix of cubic inorganic scintillators (3 cm side length), encapsulated by six plastic scintillator tiles (12 cm side length and 1 cm thickness) as shown in Figure 1. This granular architecture allows for energy deposition measurement and trajectory reconstruction, effectively acting as a compact particle telescope.

blocks.html: Plastic scintillators are chosen for their versatility as veto systems and validation triggers. While gamma-rays interact via discrete processes, charged particles exhibit continuous energy loss, allowing for effective particle identification.

This study focuses on optimizing the position reconstruction within these tiles using a data-driven approach based on Machine Learning (ML), bypassing the analytic nonlinear complexities of light transport in thin geometries. From the algorithmic standpoint the task is a regression affected by signal-dependent stochastic noise (crosstalk, afterpulsing and dark counts) and by exact symmetries of the sensor layout which render distinct impact points nearly indistinguishable.

To ensure a high degree of physical fidelity, the simulation environment was developed in Geant4, integrating experimental parameters from the EPS100 (Epic-Crystal) plastic scintillator and Onsemi FJ60035 SiPMs.

The EPS100 polystyrene-based scintillator was modeled with an emission peak at 423 nm, a decay constant of 2.4 ns, and a light output equivalent to 65% of Anthracene. Optical transport was simulated considering an attenuation length of 210 cm and a refractive index of 1.58. The tile is wrapped in a reflective coating (R = 0.95).

The SiPM response was modeled post-simulation to account for realistic noise sources. We employed a Monte Carlo hit-or-miss approach to apply the Photon Detection Efficiency (PDE) and added dark photons following a Poissonian distribution derived from the Dark Count Rate (DCR) over a 10 ns integration window [1].

Since the tile’s small thickness (1 cm) and with the aim to simulate events that leave a trace into top and bottom tiles, it is possible, as a first approximation, to limit the simulation to Minimum Ionization Particles (MIP) impinging perpendicularly. A dataset of 5 million events was generated using a diffuse perpendicularly 1 GeV muon source, providing a statistically significant basis for the training of ML models.

blocks.title: Machine Learning and Deep Learning Architectures for position reconstruction

blocks.html: The reconstruction of the MIP impact point on a single tile is formulated as a supervised regression task. For each event, the detector response is represented by the vector of SiPM signals s = [s1, . . . , s8]⊤∈R8. The regression target is the true impact coordinate on the tile plane, ˆy = [x, y]⊤, defined in a reference frame centered on the tile. To emphasize the light-distribution pattern on SiPMs and reduce sensitivity to event-to-event yield fluctuations, we adopt a normalized feature representation:

The dataset is split into training, validation, and test subsets with a 60/20/20 ratio. Preprocessing parameters, such as standardization scales, are derived exclusively from the training set to prevent data leakage. Performance is evaluated using the coordinate-wise Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) and the planar radial error (∆R), defined as:

In addition, since the true impact point is bounded to the tile active area (x, y ∈[−6, 6] cm for a 12 cm side), we introduce a soft constraint through a penalty term that discourages out-of-domain predictions:

The penalty term Lbox acts as a structural constraint, ensuring that the model learns the physical boundaries of the detector. The weight λ was empirically tuned to 2 × 104 to balance the regression accuracy and boundary adherence. Here, l = [−6, −6]⊤, h = [6, 6]⊤and ⟨·⟩denotes the batch average while ReLU(·) denotes the Rectified Linear Unit activation function, which nullifies contributions inside the admissible region and activates only when the predicted coordinate exceeds the upper bound h or falls below the lower bound l.

As a result, the penalty term is zero for physically consistent predictions and grows quadratically with the distance from the allowed domain when violations occur. This formulation ensures stable gradient-based optimization, and embeds prior geometric knowledge of the detector into the learning process without imposing hard constraints. Gradient-boosted decision trees (LightGBM). To capture non-linear dependencies between light signals and hit position, we employ a tree-ensemble regressor based on gradient boosting (LightGBM), which is wellsuited to learning non-linear interactions in tabular, lowdimensional features. The model is trained to predict the (x, y) hit coordinates via two coordinate-wise regressors, providing a competitive non-neural baseline without requiring heavy feature engineering.

To ensure the physical consistency of the Geant4 model, the simulated photon distributions were validated against experimental data obtained from cosmic ray characterization. A telescope configuration of two crossed narrow plastic scintillator detectors (finger scintillators) was employed to provide spatial triggers and localize the cosmic ray flux.

The calibration was performed by matching the Most Probable Value (MPV) of the Landau distributions across six reference impact points. This procedure allowed for the fine-tuning of the optical transport parameters, accounting for surface reflectivity and bulk attenuation. Under these conditions, the Light Collection Efficiency was determined to be approximately 2.2%, representing the ratio of optical photons detected by the SiPM array to the total scintillation yield.

A first-order reconstruction attempt was conducted using a CoG normalized likelihood approach. This method aimed to optimize the spatial weights by evaluating the expected mean photon count for each SiPM as a function of the impact position. Figure 2 illustrates the likelihood surface for a single test point.

The analysis yielded a mean reconstruction error of approximately 2 cm. This performance is considered insufficient for high-granularity space weather applications, as the likelihood function exhibits low sensitivity to spatial gradients in thin tiles, even with high-statistics training datasets.

To improve spatial resolution, we evaluated two distinct ML paradigms: a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) and a Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM). These models are theoretically capable of achieving sub-centimeter resolutions in similar scintillator geometries, with literature reporting RMSE values as low as 1 cm for MLPs [4] and 4.3 mm for LightGBM-based regressors [5].

blocks.html: Figure 3 presents the average RMSE heatmaps for all models. Color scale is the same for MLP, Constrained-MLP and LightGBM for clarity of vision.

The comparative analysis among the different approaches is summarized in Table 1, where RMSE and the 68th percentile computed on ∆R are shown. Also, the standard deviation of x and y residuals are presented. The symmetry in residual standard deviations (σ∆x ≈σ∆y) confirms the isotropic response of the algorithm.

LightGBM demonstrated superior performance across all metrics, achieving a mean radial error of 0.5659 cm. Moreover, LightGBM is the approach that requires less computation time among all. A critical observation is the divergence between ∆R and RMSE, with the latter bigger in all cases. This behavior suggests the presence of localized regions with high reconstruction error (outliers). An example of one single event reconstruction using the LightGBM is shown in Figure 4.

While CoG approach presents the worst performances with a good reconstruction only in the central region or in the SiPMs proximity, all ML models exhibit similar spatial error patterns. Specifically, the resolution degrades significantly at the tile boundaries due to "blind spots" (regions with poor geometric acceptance by the SiPMs). Additionally, four symmetrical regions along the diagonals show increased radial error. This is interpreted as a geometric degeneracy: the high symmetry of the SiPM layout produces nearly identical photon hit patterns for distinct impact points, complicating the discrimination between direct and reflected optical paths.

blocks.html: Notably, while LightGBM provides superior performance at the boundaries, the MLP-based models exhibit higher reconstruction stability in the central region (|x, y| < 4 cm). This spatial complementarity suggests that events at the edges are better reconstructed by the decisiontree logic of LightGBM, whereas the smooth functional mapping of the MLP is ideal for the central isotropic region. This suggests the use a Mixture of Expert approach using two models: LightGBM for boundaries and Constrained- MLP for the central zone.

To better investigate the differences in the two models, scatter plots of True vs Predicted positions for x and y are shown in Figure 5 both for Constrained-MLP and LightGBM. It is possible to observe that the performances are very similar along the whole tile surface but the very central point (position (0,0)) in which Constrained-MLP reconstructs slightly better the impinging position obtaining, however, a greater RMSE mean value along the tile. Moreover, LightGBM reconstructs some events outside the tile surface due to the non implementation of a loss function that penalize event reconstructed outside the tile geometric dimensions.

blocks.caption: Spatial RMSE distribution along x and y axis for the MLP 5a and LightGBM 5b models. Even if LightGBM offers better performances, some points are reconstructed outside the tile. This behavior is not present in the MLP reconstruction.
blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: The transition from CoG-based to ML-driven reconstruction has yielded a significant improvement in spatial resolution, with LightGBM emerging as the most effective architecture with high performances, low errors and fast computation. However, the presence of geometric degeneracies and edge effects remains a limiting factor.
Future developments will focus on:

1. Temporal Feature Integration: Integrating the Time-of-Arrival (ToA) of the photons can break the geometric symmetry. Recent studies [6] suggest that incorporating timing information can reduce the RMSE by up to 24%;

The average RMSE values are computed as the mean value among all events in a bin of 1 mm size. 3b, 3c and 3d present same color scale for visual clarification.
blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: 2. Geometric Optimization: We propose to evaluate asymmetric SiPM configurations to minimize the spatial degeneracies observed in the current layout;

3. Mixture of Experts: The best performances are obtained in the central region (from -4 to 4 cm) with the Constrained-MLP approach while LightGBM is the best methodology for boundaries. With the aim to achieve the best possible resolution in the whole tile we are focused on the exploitation of a Mixture of Experts (MoE) approach, in which the two different approaches are managed by an higher level AI that manages the two models.
The validated models will be integrated into the onboard processing pipeline of the CubeSat payload to evaluate their real-time performance in high-rate environments.
